objective: Give the package list a smooth scroll: a wheel notch becomes a movement, not a jump. And prove it, because the pointer events of this desktop never reach the running application.

what_changed.the_wheel: The list container takes the wheel before the list applies it. The distance is taken back from the list, kept, and handed over eased, frame by frame. The two cancel out whichever order the handlers run in, so the mechanism does not depend on the dispatch order.
what_changed.the_easing: A frame gives back 22% of the waiting distance. The last frame gives the remainder back whole, so the list lands exactly where the wheel asked. The waiting distance is bounded to 240 px, so a long scroll cannot leave the list behind by a mile.
what_changed.the_frame_loop: The view asks for the next frame itself, with cx.notify(). window.request_animation_frame() would notify the enclosing view instead of this one, and panics when the view is laid out on its own.
what_changed.also: The same frame request was corrected in the sidebar and in the operation console, which had the same latent hazard.

the_crash_the_proof_found.what: window.request_animation_frame() inside a view's render panics with 'called Option::unwrap() on a None value' at gpui/src/window.rs:3363 when the view is laid out on its own.
the_crash_the_proof_found.why: gpui's Entity::request_layout calls the view's render outside the rendered-view stack, and request_animation_frame() asks the window for the current view, which is then None.
the_crash_the_proof_found.where_it_mattered: Three places: the workstation's new smooth scroll, the sidebar's collapse animation, the operation console's drawer animation. The two older ones never crashed in the running application because they are always laid out inside another view, but they notified the enclosing view instead of themselves.
the_crash_the_proof_found.the_fix: cx.notify() — the view asks for its own next frame.

the_proof.how: gpui's own event system: a window, a real wheel event, a real hit test, the real bubble order. The scroller is a scrollable div, which is the same gpui machinery a uniform list is made of.
what_it_asserts: after the wheel, the list has not moved: the notch does not make it jump
after one frame, the list has moved a fraction of the distance (22%, between 30 and 60 px of 200)
after forty frames, the list is exactly where the wheel asked: -200 px, within 1 px
the_unit_tests: the_smooth_scroll_gives_the_distance_back_in_several_frames: the distance comes back over twenty-odd frames, and all of it
the_pending_distance_is_bounded: the waiting distance is clamped to 240 px in both directions

the_gaps.the_harness_cannot_lay_out_the_applicati: The application's list is a uniform list, whose measured layout never resolves in gpui 0.2.2's test harness: the list keeps zero bounds, has no hitbox, and cannot scroll. The proof is therefore made on the same structure with a scrollable div, and the application's own list is not exercised by it.
the_gaps.the_running_application_is_not_exercised: Synthetic pointer events never reach the Wayland client on this desktop, so the feel of the scroll — the twenty frames, the weight — is not verified by the hand. The numbers are verified; the feel is the user's to judge.
the_gaps.the_release_build_is_not_in_the_gate_run: The gate was run with --quick, which skips the two release builds; the release build of the application was produced separately with the same toolchain and the same lock.

artefacts.note: the run's scratch now lives in .ci-cache/tmp, not in the shared tmpfs: a suite that writes its scratch there can fail with ENOSPC because of somebody else's leftovers, which looks exactly like a failure of the code.

the_gate.also: the tmpfs of the machine was at 100% (16 Go of stale shell scratch, and a live session of another project); 4.1 Go were freed after checking that no live process held any of it, and the run's scratch was moved into the repository.
